Tests with correlated latent variables in simulated data

Source: R/simulate.R
probit_dependence.Rd

probit_dependence() makes the simulated test results dependent given the disease status by giving each test a normal latent variable and letting these variables be correlated, with one correlation for each pair of tests and disease class. The correlations can have any sign, separately for each pair. The sensitivity and specificity of each test do not change: the correlations change only how often the tests are right or wrong together. The object is passed to simulate_study() as its dependence argument.

Usage

probit_dependence(diseased_correlation = 0, healthy_correlation = 0)

Arguments

diseased_correlation

Correlations \(R_1\) between the latent variables of the tests among the diseased: either a single number, the same correlation for every pair of tests, or a symmetric \(K \times K\) matrix with 1 on the diagonal, whose rows and columns follow the order of the sensitivity argument of simulate_study(). Values in \([-1, 1]\). Default 0: the tests are independent among the diseased. The size of the matrix and its positive definiteness (which excludes, for example, a single number equal to 1 with two or more tests) are checked when the data are simulated.

healthy_correlation

Correlations \(R_0\) between the latent variables of the tests among the healthy, with the same form as diseased_correlation. Default 0: the tests are independent among the healthy.

Value

An object of class probit_dependence.

Details

Given the disease status \(D = d\), the \(K\) tests have latent variables \(Y = (Y_1, \dots, Y_K)\) jointly normal with mean 0, variance 1 and correlation matrix \(R_d\) (diseased_correlation for \(d = 1\), healthy_correlation for \(d = 0\)). Test \(k\) is positive when $$Y_k < \Phi^{-1}(Se_k) \textrm{ if } d = 1, \qquad Y_k < \Phi^{-1}(1 - Sp_k) \textrm{ if } d = 0,$$ where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal distribution function, so that \(P(T_k = 1 \mid D = 1) = Se_k\) and \(P(T_k = 0 \mid D = 0) = Sp_k\) exactly, whatever the correlations. Probit models of this kind for conditional dependence are studied by Qu et al. (1996) and Dendukuri and Joseph (2001).

The element \(R_{d,jk}\) is the correlation between the latent variables of tests \(j\) and \(k\) in class \(d\) (known as the tetrachoric correlation of the two results). Positive values make the two tests agree more often than under independence, negative values less often, and 0 makes their results uncorrelated. For example, two tests with sensitivity 0.8 and correlation 0.5 among the diseased have an odds ratio of about 4.7 between their results; with correlation 0.8, about 19. With all the correlations of a class equal to 0 the tests are independent in that class.

A correlation matrix must be positive definite: not every set of pairwise correlations is possible. For example, the same correlation \(r\) for all pairs of \(K\) tests needs \(-1/(K - 1) < r < 1\), so with three tests \(r > -1/2\). Since \(K\) is known only when the data are simulated, this condition is checked by simulate_study(), which gives an error for a matrix that is not positive definite.

References

Dendukuri, N. and Joseph, L. (2001). Bayesian approaches to modeling the conditional dependence between multiple diagnostic tests. Biometrics, 57(1), 158–167. doi:10.1111/j.0006-341X.2001.00158.x

Qu, Y., Tan, M. and Kutner, M. H. (1996). Random effects models in latent class analysis for evaluating accuracy of diagnostic tests. Biometrics, 52(3), 797–810. doi:10.2307/2533043

See also

simulate_study(), independence(), latent_dependence()

Examples

# correlation 0.4 between every pair among the diseased, 0.2 among the healthy
probit_dependence(diseased_correlation = 0.4, healthy_correlation = 0.2)
#> <probit_dependence> tests with correlated latent variables
#>   diseased_correlation: 0.4
#>   healthy_correlation: 0.2

# different correlation for each pair: A and B positively correlated,
# C negatively correlated with both
R1 <- matrix(c( 1,    0.5, -0.3,
                0.5,  1,   -0.3,
               -0.3, -0.3,  1), 3, 3)
d <- simulate_study(n = 2000, prevalence = 0.3,
                    sensitivity = c(A = 0.9, B = 0.8, C = 0.7),
                    specificity = c(A = 0.85, B = 0.9, C = 0.95),
                    verification_prob = 1,
                    dependence = probit_dependence(diseased_correlation = R1))
sick <- d$disease == 1
cor(d[sick, c("A", "B", "C")])
#>             A           B           C
#> A  1.00000000  0.16611978 -0.09133949
#> B  0.16611978  1.00000000 -0.07316651
#> C -0.09133949 -0.07316651  1.00000000

# every pair negatively correlated: possible with three tests if r > -1/2
probit_dependence(diseased_correlation = -0.3)
#> <probit_dependence> tests with correlated latent variables
#>   diseased_correlation: -0.3
#>   healthy_correlation: 0
